title: What Feels Normal to You?
summary: Explore cultural values as colleagues prepare for a shared review.
learningObjective: Explore cultural values as colleagues prepare for a shared review.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Here's a meeting you might recognize. One colleague wants a draft to read first. Another wants to talk before anyone writes. A manager needs a recommendation, and a partner wants time to consult their team. Who's approaching the work the right way?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd say we need more information. Each approach could help. The difficulty starts when my preferred way quietly becomes the rule for everyone else.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: That's what this course invites us to notice. Cultural values can help us ask better questions about our expectations. They don't tell us what someone believes because of their race, background, disability, age, or role.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: So, if a partner wants to consult colleagues, I can ask whose input they need and how much time would help. I shouldn't assume they can't make a decision.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Yes. That's one way to explore individual and collective priorities. Authority is another lens. Someone may expect a manager to decide and still have an important concern to raise. We can explain who decides and offer a usable way to question the information.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: A quiet meeting doesn't necessarily mean agreement. Written input or a private follow-up might reveal something the discussion missed.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Let's return to that request for a draft. How might uncertainty and time horizons affect what people need?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: A draft can make the task more predictable. A conversation can help us discover what belongs in it. And while I'm thinking about Friday's deadline, a partner may be thinking about how the guidance will work for the next six months.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Both matter. We can settle what needs a decision now and agree when to revisit what remains uncertain. We don't need to label one person resistant and the other adaptable.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: The course also asks us to think about cooperation, competition, being, and doing. What would those look like in this review?

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Look at what gets recognized. The final presentation may get attention, while careful listening or checking access needs goes unnoticed. We can value those contributions and still be clear about each person's responsibilities.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: Communication is where I often notice differences. Some people say the concern directly. Others expect us to understand it from the situation. How can we handle that respectfully?

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Check what you understood. You might say, I want to make sure I haven't missed your concern. Is the review time too short? Important instructions should be clear enough that people don't have to guess.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: And visible emotion isn't a shortcut to understanding. A quiet voice doesn't prove indifference, and a forceful voice doesn't settle whether someone's reasoning is sound.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Exactly. Ask about the concern. Then consider common rules and particular circumstances. Where is flexibility available, and how can someone request it fairly? A personal connection shouldn't be the only route to extra time.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: The same applies to time and scheduling. What looks like a preference for overlapping tasks could be a workload problem. A missed meeting could involve transportation or caregiving. Ask about the actual constraint before calling it culture.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: We've touched all ten lenses in the course. Let's use them to improve the review: a short draft beforehand, time for written comments, a focused discussion, and a clear decision. Which part would help your team?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd start by asking: would a written outline help you prepare, or do we need to talk something through first? That's a question a person can answer for themselves.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Take a moment to write a question like that for your own work. Then check the requirements and agree on an arrangement. You can pause here and return when you're ready.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: Afterward, ask whether people could contribute and understood the decision. We don't have to share every preference to work well together. We need curiosity, clear expectations, and a willingness to adjust what isn't helping.
